newsitem.title: USA: Russian doctors come to U.S. to learn.
newsitem.headline: Russian doctors come to U.S. to learn.

text.p: Health care spending in the United States is 40 times what it is in Russia, and a delegation of Russian doctors said on Tuesday they wanted to find how to improve their woeful position.
"We are surviving on enthusiasm," Moscow surgeon A.G. Sarkisyan said of his fellow physicians and nurses.

Sarkisyan headed a delegation of doctors from the four-year-old Russian Medical Association visiting the American Medical Association headquarters in Chicago for briefings under a U.S. State Department grant.
"The salary we receive is not enough to even travel to work," he said in an interview. "We are the only people who can solve our problems. We have come to learn."

The Russian group was the first of two delegations to meet with U.S. government officials, tour hospital facilities and gain insight into the lobbying power of the American Medical Association and other U.S. physicians groups.

They said their primary aim was to learn how to attract the Russian public's attention to their plight ahead of the planned June meeting of the Pirogov Congress of Physicians. The congresses began in the last century but were suspended after the communist takeover and only resumed in 1995.

The physicians said Russia's hard-pressed budget under President Boris Yeltsin had slashed financing of the medical system to about one-quarter of one percent of Russia's Gross National Product from about one-third of one percent, compared to U.S. health care spending of roughly 15 percent of U.S. GNP.
When Yeltsin underwent heart surgery at Moscow's Cardiology Research Centre, the uncut grass outside the faded communist-era showplace testified to its financial woes.

Russia and the United States have a similar number of physicians, but American doctors are highly organised and set policy and accredit its members in a democratic fashion, Sarkisyan said admiringly. He said the Russians were also hoping to develop a system for accrediting medical schools and licensing doctors, some of whom are incompetent.

"Russian medicine is in crisis and one of the reasons is a sharp decrease in (government) funding," said Timothy Flaherty, a member of the AMA board of trustees who has travelled to Russia and witnessed hospital conditions there.
"They do have universal access to health care, but there are a number of hospitals without running water."
